newsitem.title: BARBADOS: CRICKET-AMBROSE HAS 300 TEST WICKETS MARK IN SIGHT.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-AMBROSE HAS 300 TEST WICKETS MARK IN SIGHT.

text.p: Curtly Ambrose will have 300 test wickets in his sights when spearheading West Indies' attack during the third test against India starting on Thursday.
Ambrose, a man of few words but whose deeds speak volumes for his high-quality fast bowling, has captured 290 wickets in his 67 tests.

After going wicketless in the drawn first test of the five-match series in Kingston, Jamaica, Ambrose took five for 87 in India's only innings during the second draw of the rubber at Port of Spain, Trinidad.
Ambrose is on the way to becoming the fourth West Indies' bowler to reach the 300 test wickets landmark behind Malcolm Marshall, current captain Courtney Walsh and Lance Gibbs.

Though the Kensington Oval pitch may lack the great pace of former years, Ambrose's ability to extract a measure of life from any surface can offer West Indies their most realistic chance to break the series deadlock.
With Ian Bishop back in a squad of 13 after injury kept him out of the second test, West Indies hope to have a full hand of fast bowlers to choose from.

Walsh complained of a sore hamstring in Jamaica's Red Stripe Cup match at the weekend but, if this clears up quickly, he will join Ambrose and Bishop in an attack to be completed by Franklyn Rose or Mervyn Dillon, assuming West Indies stick to their traditional formula of four pacemen.
Rose made an impressive arrival on the test scene with a seven-wicket match haul at Kingston, and Dillon took three for 92 on his debut at Port of Spain.
In contrast to their opponents, India's most telling weapon has been the leg spin of Anil Kumble.

Kumble has taken a haul of 15 wickets in the first two tests, helping to offset the loss of their best pace bowler, Javagal Srinath, whose tour was cut short by a torn shoulder muscle before the series started.
After taking a first innings lead of 140 and making West Indies work relatively hard to save the second test on the final day, India face the Bridgetown match with confidence lifted.
They will also be aware that West Indies do not quite have their previous aura of invincibility at Kensington Oval, once the Caribbean cricket stronghold.

West Indies went 59 years without losing a test in Bridgetown until they were beaten by England in 1994 and Australia in 1995, though victory over New Zealand last year helped to restore a degree of pride.
